body:
## Why start with the first touch?
Any player who receives the ball and controls it with the first touch gains an extra second to think before an opponent arrives — and that second is often the difference between a successful pass and losing the ball. The drills below suit young players aged 6 to 12, and need nothing more than a ball and a small space.

## 1. Cushion Control
The player throws the ball to themselves or to a teammate and receives it with the inside or top of the foot so it stops close by, without bouncing away. Repeat with both feet, then later with the chest and thigh.

**Coaching tip:** Ask the player to receive the ball with their eyes up, looking forward, not down. This early habit builds the field awareness (scanning) that's much harder to teach later on.

## 2. Directional First Touch
Instead of stopping the ball dead, the player receives it and redirects it at a simple angle away from an imaginary defender (a cone or ground marker). The goal: get out of pressure in a single touch.

## 3. Control Under Pressure
A lightly-moving defender (or a teammate) stands two meters away, and the player tries to receive the ball and move it out of reach within two seconds. This drill raises decision-making speed under real pressure, not just in an ideal setting.

## 4. Receiving with the Weak Foot
The same cushion-control drills, but with the weaker foot only. Most young players avoid this naturally, and that's exactly where early repetition makes a big difference a few years down the line.

## 5. Wall Passes
If a wall is available, repeat passing and receiving with one or two touches at increasing speed. This drill combines passing accuracy with control speed, using the least possible space and equipment.

## Summary for coaches and parents
There's no need for a long daily session; 10-15 minutes of these drills, 3-4 times a week, is enough to build a real technical foundation before moving on to more complex exercises. Consistency matters more than intensity here.
